rules.name: incremental_feature_config_sweep
rules.context: When hyperparameters are already tuned or the model is established, and you suspect the feature configuration (e.g., vocabulary size, aggregation functions) is suboptimal relative to dataset characteristics.
rules.action: Change one feature-configuration lever at a time (e.g., one max_features value or one aggregation function). Submit or check CV after each change. If the new setting degrades score, revert before trying the next option. Avoid stacking multiple untested feature changes simultaneously, as confounding makes it hard to isolate which change helped or hurt.
rules.exceptions: Both source items note that authors sometimes changed two things at once (alpha + max_features; var + removing 'last'), confounding results. The rule is aspirational—strict isolation is not always followed in practice.

rules.name: reverse_direction_on_regression_then_reduce_step
rules.context: During a leaderboard hyperparameter or blend-weight sweep, a parameter change causes a clear score drop compared to the previous best.
rules.action: Immediately reverse the direction of the parameter change, moving back toward the last best value with a smaller step size. Do not explore further in the regression direction unless there is a strong theoretical reason. If the reversal recovers or improves the score, bracket the optimum within a narrow range and stop.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_weight_sweep_on_diminishing_returns
rules.context: When tuning ensemble blend weights between models of similar quality, the first one or two weight adjustments yield negligible improvement (e.g., <0.001 on the target metric).
rules.action: Abandon the blend-weight sweep after one or two steps. Switch effort to a qualitatively different lever—such as adding a new diverse model, improving individual model quality, or changing architecture—rather than continuing fine-grained weight tuning.
rules.exceptions: If the auxiliary model is much weaker, a narrow micro-weight sweep (1-2% region, ~8 trials max) may still be worthwhile before stopping (29588171:e1#1).

rules.name: revert_and_isolate_after_multi_change_regression
rules.context: Multiple changes (e.g., architecture + hyperparameters, optimizer + bug fix, checkpoint + kernel size) were bundled in one submission and the leaderboard score regressed.
rules.action: Revert to the last known good configuration. Then re-apply each change individually in separate submissions to isolate the cause. Prioritize reverting the most disruptive/speculative change first while keeping clearly correct fixes. Do not continue building on the regressed version. Limit to 2-3 isolation submissions before deciding.
rules.exceptions: When one change is clearly beneficial (e.g., a bug fix) and another is speculative, you can selectively revert only the speculative component rather than reverting everything (77129691:e11#1).

rules.name: stop_after_two_consecutive_null_or_regressing_probes
rules.context: Two successive probes of the same lever (e.g., escalating a hyperparameter, ablating components, or tuning a preprocessing toggle) both show no improvement or increasing regression.
rules.action: Revert to the best-known configuration and abandon that lever. Move on to an orthogonal lever rather than continuing to probe in the same direction. Do not spend more than two submissions confirming what two data points already show.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: bundle_high_confidence_fixes_to_save_submissions
rules.context: Multiple fixes are identified where each has high confidence of being correct (e.g., matching known training settings like resolution and normalization), and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Bundle all high-confidence fixes into a single submission rather than testing each independently. Only isolate changes when the direction of effect is uncertain or when you need to attribute improvement to a specific change.
rules.exceptions: Bundling makes attribution impossible; if one change could plausibly be harmful, test separately (15082684:e4#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: test_new_model_with_minimal_other_changes
rules.context: Introducing a new model architecture, backbone, or checkpoint variant into an existing pipeline.
rules.action: Swap only the model/checkpoint while keeping all other pipeline components (post-processing, ensemble weights, preprocessing) identical. Submit to get a clean signal. If it regresses, try one alternative checkpoint before reverting the architecture entirely. Do not combine the model swap with other untested changes.
rules.exceptions: 13848868:e5#1 notes that post-processing preferences may not transfer across models, so after the clean model swap, also test toggling post-processing on/off for the new model.

rules.name: revert_large_feature_batch_after_regression
rules.context: A large batch of new features was added and the leaderboard score regressed, and one or two compensating tweaks (loss tuning, postprocessing) fail to recover the prior best.
rules.action: Revert the feature addition entirely rather than continuing to tune around it. Do not spend more than two recovery attempts. If you believe some features are valuable, add them in smaller subsets in future experiments.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e24#1 suggests that if you can confirm value by ablation (removing only the new features causes regression), keep them—but if recovery attempts fail, revert.

rules.name: checkpoint_and_move_on_after_clear_improvement
rules.context: A single experiment yields a clear new best score, and there are other orthogonal levers (new features, new models) to explore.
rules.action: Record the result with version logs documenting the baseline score, checkpoint the code, and move on to the next orthogonal lever rather than immediately grid-searching around the successful hyperparameters. Return to fine-tuning later if needed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablate_ensemble_member_before_tuning
rules.context: An ensemble has multiple members and you suspect one is weaker or its contribution is uncertain.
rules.action: Disable the suspected weaker member and submit the remaining prediction to measure marginal contribution. If the single/reduced model matches or beats the ensemble, drop the weaker member permanently. If it regresses, restore the ensemble and tune the weaker member or seek better diversity sources instead.
rules.exceptions: 27502740:e4#2 notes that if blending same-framework models hurts, seek diversity from a genuinely different source rather than abandoning blending entirely.

rules.name: retune_blend_weights_after_ensemble_composition_change
rules.context: The composition of an ensemble has changed (models added, removed, or retrained) and blend weights were tuned for the old composition.
rules.action: Re-probe the blend weight by shifting it moderately from the previous best (e.g., ±0.10). If the first probe improves, accept it; if not, try the opposite direction. One or two probes usually suffice. Do not over-tune on a small public leaderboard—if redistribution causes regression, revert to previous weights and invest in improving base models instead.
rules.exceptions: 18851026:e4#2 warns against over-tuning when the public test set is very small.

rules.name: binary_toggle_test_for_uncertain_config
rules.context: A single binary configuration choice (filter, preprocessing toggle, post-processing on/off) is in question and its effect is uncertain.
rules.action: Disable the setting, submit, compare to the previous score. If the score regresses, immediately re-enable and submit to confirm recovery. Two submissions answer the question definitively. For binary toggles, evaluate locally (OOF) first if possible; submit both variants to leaderboard only if local signal is ambiguous.
rules.exceptions: 75584724:e5#1 notes that local OOF signal may be insufficient for noisy metrics, requiring LB confirmation of both states.

rules.name: quick_feasibility_probe_before_model_family_swap
rules.context: The current model family has plateaued or regressed despite hyperparameter tuning, and you want to try a fundamentally different approach.
rules.action: Run a quick probe with the alternative model on a small number of folds without submitting. Check that the model is compatible with the task (e.g., regression vs classification) and produces valid predictions. If the probe fails or produces clearly worse results, revert immediately. Keep the probe to one or two versions before deciding.
rules.exceptions: 7676170:e4#1 warns that hasty probes can miss fundamental mismatches (e.g., using a classifier for regression); verify task compatibility before coding.

rules.name: verify_inference_changes_before_submitting
rules.context: A change affects all predictions at inference time (e.g., TTA, dropout, scaling) and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Add per-sample debug prints or logging for the new inference path, run without submitting to inspect outputs for sanity (reasonable ranges, no degenerate values). Only submit after confirming outputs look reasonable. This avoids wasting submissions on broken inference.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: isolate_single_change_per_submission
rules.context: When testing multiple new ideas (e.g., new checkpoint + hyperparameter change, new feature + new metric) and each leaderboard submission is costly or limited.
rules.action: Change only one lever per submission so regressions can be attributed. If you bundled changes and regressed, partially revert the most suspicious change first. If two consecutive bundled submissions both regress, revert fully to the last known best before trying anything else.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very tight and one change is expected to dominate the effect (e.g., major hyperparameter overhaul vs. minor feature cleanup), bundling is acceptable per 27836972:e13#2.

rules.name: revert_before_layering_on_regression
rules.context: When a change (checkpoint swap, feature removal, new component) causes a leaderboard regression and you want to test an orthogonal new idea.
rules.action: Test the new idea on top of the last-known-best configuration, not on top of the regressed version. Stacking an unproven change on an already-regressed baseline makes attribution impossible. Revert first, then apply the new idea in isolation.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_ablation_for_multi_change_regression
rules.context: When a commit that introduced multiple changes (new layer/component + hyperparameter change) causes a large regression, and you need to identify the culprit.
rules.action: Revert the most novel or structurally risky component first (e.g., new architectural layer) while keeping the simpler changes (e.g., fold count). If performance recovers, the component was harmful—do not re-introduce it. Submit only after confirming recovery.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: gate_risky_changes_on_local_cv
rules.context: When probing a fundamentally different model, architecture, or speculative preprocessing change whose impact is uncertain and leaderboard submissions are limited.
rules.action: Do not submit until local CV confirms the change is at least competitive with the current best. Fix runtime issues first, then evaluate on validation. Only submit after CV scores match or exceed the current LB baseline. If CV is disappointing, abandon the probe without burning a submission.
rules.exceptions: When local CV is unreliable (very small dataset, high CV-LB divergence), a direct LB probe may be necessary.

rules.name: retest_cheap_toggles_after_model_change
rules.context: When you have a cheap binary post-processing toggle (e.g., rank conversion, normalization flag) or a blending weight whose optimal value was previously established, but you have since changed the underlying model or ensemble composition.
rules.action: Re-test both states of the toggle (or previously discarded parameter values) after every model/ensemble change, as the optimal setting can shift. Submit both and keep whichever scores higher. Do not assume the previous winner carries over.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_speculative_probe_on_first_regression
rules.context: When a speculative preprocessing or data augmentation change (e.g., text cleaning on pretrained encoders, SMOTE oversampling) is tested as a single probe and the leaderboard score regresses.
rules.action: Revert immediately rather than tuning the parameters of the failed approach. If the direction is wrong on the first try, parameter tuning is unlikely to save it. Do not invest multiple iterations refining an approach that hurt initially.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is very small and confounded by other simultaneous changes, a second isolated test may be warranted.

rules.name: swap_backbone_diversity_over_weight_tuning
rules.context: When fine-tuning ensemble blend weights yields diminishing returns (negligible or negative improvement) and the ensemble contains multiple models from the same architecture family.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights and instead swap the weakest-contributing member for a backbone from a different model family (e.g., replace a RoBERTa variant with DeBERTa). Architectural diversity typically yields larger gains than optimizing blend coefficients among similar models.
rules.exceptions: If a non-linear blending formula (e.g., power-mean) hasn't been tried yet, it may yield a quick marginal gain before switching to backbone diversity.

rules.name: isolate_checkpoint_swap_from_hyperparameter_change
rules.context: When swapping a pretrained checkpoint that may have been trained with different settings than the current inference hyperparameters assume.
rules.action: First submit with the original hyperparameters to isolate the checkpoint effect. Only after confirming the checkpoint works, change one hyperparameter at a time. Never change both checkpoint and architecture hyperparameters simultaneously, as a regression becomes undiagnosable.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_ablation_via_pruning
rules.context: When you have a complex ensemble with many weighted members and want to understand which components are actually contributing to performance.
rules.action: Submit a drastically pruned version (1-2 members) to the leaderboard. If it regresses significantly, ensemble diversity is valuable—keep or expand members. If it matches or improves, many members are redundant and you should simplify. Limit to 1-2 ablation submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_sweeping_after_structural_change_reprobe
rules.context: When you have already extensively swept a hyperparameter, then made a structural change to the pipeline, and a single re-probe near the old optimum confirms improvement.
rules.action: Accept the re-probed value and move on to a different lever rather than re-sweeping the full range. Diminishing returns are likely since the prior sweep already mapped the landscape and the structural change is unlikely to have dramatically shifted the optimum.
rules.exceptions: If the structural change fundamentally alters the prediction distribution (e.g., adding a new model family to the ensemble), a broader re-sweep may be warranted.

rules.name: revert_extreme_parameter_and_pivot
rules.context: When a parameter change is so extreme it causes runtime failure or nonsensical results (e.g., n_splits nearly equal to dataset size).
rules.action: Do not try to fix incrementally. Reset the problematic parameter to a reasonable value and pivot to the next experiment. Bundle the fix with a new idea to save a version/submission.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_regression_before_next_change
rules.context: When exploring multiple hyperparameters or model configurations and a change produces a score regression compared to the current baseline.
rules.action: Revert the regressing change before trying the next modification. Change only one thing per submission and measure each change against a fixed baseline. Do not stack untested changes—if two things changed and the score dropped, you cannot attribute the cause. If regression persists after 2-3 isolated attempts, shift strategy (e.g., move to ensembling or a different model family).
rules.exceptions: In 29588171, the author failed to revert regressions before trying the next change, making attribution impossible and prolonging the regression. In 28984551, model-family switching only partially recovered; real recovery came from ensembling rather than single-model tuning.

rules.name: revert_capacity_increase_on_regression
rules.context: When tuning model capacity parameters (tree depth/leaves, backbone size, channel width) by small increments and the first increase over a moderate baseline causes a score regression.
rules.action: Revert to the original capacity setting rather than trying further increases. Try 2-3 configurations at most; if none improves over baseline, the capacity direction is wrong. For GBDT with ordinal objectives, prefer conservative tree capacity. For CNN attention blocks, a gap >0.5% AUC after 3 configs suggests the architecture variant itself is inferior.
rules.exceptions: Only increasing capacity was tested in the GBDT case; decreasing below baseline was never tried. In the CNN case, backbone changes confounded the comparison.

rules.name: estimate_blend_impact_before_tuning
rules.context: When tuning hyperparameters of a model that contributes a small fraction (<5%) of an ensemble blend weight, and the ensemble is dominated by strong external or other submissions.
rules.action: Before tuning, estimate the maximum possible score improvement given the blend weight. If the model's weight is too low for improvements to be visible on the leaderboard, either increase the model's blend weight first or redirect effort to the dominant ensemble components.
rules.exceptions: In the EEG/spectrogram case the secondary branch was not blended by weight but architecturally integrated, so the principle applies loosely—the spectrogram preprocessing mattered more than EEG branch sizing.

rules.name: probe_baseline_with_repeated_submissions
rules.context: When starting with a pipeline whose true leaderboard performance is unknown—either because the training algorithm is stochastic (e.g., DART dropout) or because the pipeline depends on external artifacts with no local validation score.
rules.action: Submit the unchanged pipeline multiple times (at least 2–3, up to 5–10 for highly stochastic methods) to establish a reliable baseline and measure run-to-run variance. Use the observed score range as the noise floor / minimum detectable effect size. Only treat subsequent changes as improvements if they exceed this noise band. Stop re-submitting once 3+ consecutive scores converge.
rules.exceptions: For DART-based models, 9 re-submissions may be excessive; 4–5 may suffice once scores stabilize (28834369 counter_evidence).

rules.name: pivot_lever_when_score_range_negligible
rules.context: When exhausting the natural variants of a lever (e.g., checkpoint subsets, small config changes) produces score differences smaller than leaderboard noise or the observed noise band from probe runs.
rules.action: Stop iterating on the current lever. Pivot to a qualitatively different lever with higher potential variance in outcomes (e.g., different model family, different feature set, pipeline replacement). Reserve incremental tuning for when the baseline is already within a few points of the target.
rules.exceptions: When the gap to competitive scores is small (<2–3 points), incremental tuning of the same lever may still be worthwhile (13577502:e1#2 implies this threshold).

rules.name: isolate_changes_on_regression
rules.context: A submission that bundles multiple changes (e.g., feature selection, hyperparameters, post-processing) regresses on the leaderboard, making it impossible to attribute the drop to a single change.
rules.action: Revert the most speculative changes first (novel post-processing, hyperparameter tweaks) while keeping the structural addition under test. Submit the simpler variant to isolate the new component's effect. Only after confirming its value, layer additional changes back in via 3-5 systematic partial-configuration submissions.
rules.exceptions: In practice, authors sometimes succeed by combining multiple changes in a single submission (e.g., 60197293 v130), so strict one-at-a-time isolation may be relaxed when submission budget is tight and the combined changes are well-understood.

rules.name: replace_flat_preprocessing_sweep_with_model_regularization
rules.context: Sweeping a preprocessing hyperparameter (e.g., feature-selection threshold) shows the model is insensitive across a wide range of values, and the model has built-in equivalents (e.g., LightGBM's feature_fraction, bagging_fraction).
rules.action: Remove the manual preprocessing step and rely on the model's native regularization controls instead. This reduces pipeline complexity and frees the search budget for higher-impact levers. If the sweep showed a clear optimum, keep the preprocessing; only drop it when the response surface is flat or noisy.
rules.exceptions: Only demonstrated within a single competition (amex-default-prediction); may not generalize when the preprocessing step addresses a problem the model cannot handle natively.

rules.name: avoid_broad_feature_removal_from_regularized_gbdt
rules.context: When using a well-regularized GBDT (with feature subsampling, bagging, early stopping) and you suspect broad categories of engineered features (e.g., all max/min aggregations, or permutation-importance-flagged features) are adding noise.
rules.action: Do not manually remove broad categories of engineered features by name pattern or a single importance run. If a targeted exclusion regresses the score, revert it. Instead, if importance-based removal hurts, regenerate importance with a different seed/method, compare lists, and only drop features consistently ranked unimportant across runs. The model's built-in regularization handles most irrelevant features.
rules.exceptions: Feature-selection ratio tuning (e.g., keeping top 50%) can still help; the rule applies to categorical exclusion by feature-name pattern or a single noisy importance ranking.

rules.name: sweep_feature_count_threshold_bidirectionally
rules.context: When using high-dimensional features (e.g., TF-IDF) with an importance-based feature count cutoff and the current cutoff already produces a competitive score.
rules.action: Sweep the feature count in both directions from the current value using a fixed step (e.g., ±500–1000). If both directions degrade the score, the current value is near-optimal—stop sweeping and move to a different lever (e.g., adding new raw features or toggling feature selection on/off). When adding new feature sources, test with and without feature selection enabled to determine if the selection list is too restrictive for the new features.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: drop_high_na_or_redundant_columns_before_engineering
rules.context: When a block of raw features is either predominantly missing or represents the same underlying concept at multiple granularities (e.g., matching scores at different resolutions), and downstream aggregations or models inherit this redundancy/noise.
rules.action: Remove the entire block of high-NA or redundant-resolution raw columns before computing derived features (aggregations, encodings). This eliminates multiple noisy derived features at once, reducing memory and noise. Verify via validation before submitting. This is complementary to post-hoc importance-based pruning.
rules.exceptions: If the redundant columns are only used in a subset of model components (e.g., removed from one sub-model but kept in another), the benefit may be partial.

rules.name: explicit_interactions_redundant_for_gbdt_with_rich_features
rules.context: When using a GBDT model on a tabular dataset with many available features, and considering adding explicit pairwise interaction features (e.g., differences, ratios) or handcrafted domain features on top of an already rich feature representation.
rules.action: Treat explicit interaction/handcrafted features as low-priority since GBDTs and transformer embeddings already capture such interactions internally. If you try them, add as a single probe submission and compare CV/LB. Expect diminishing or negative returns. Be prepared to revert quickly rather than investing many iterations in narrowing subsets.
rules.exceptions: When the model uses a very small feature subset or lacks the capacity to learn the interaction, explicit features may still help (see 28093671:e8#1 where expanding features helped).

rules.name: expand_feature_set_before_engineering_interactions
rules.context: When a GBDT model uses a small manually-selected subset of available features and scores poorly, before investing in crafting interaction or derived features.
rules.action: Progressively expand the feature set by adding batches of unused features ordered by importance, validating each expansion. Simultaneously simplify unnecessary preprocessing (imputation, scaling, outlier removal) that GBDTs handle natively. Only after the feature set is comprehensive should you consider adding engineered interaction features.
rules.exceptions: When all available features are already included (as in 27836972:e9#1), expansion is not possible and interaction engineering becomes the natural next step—though it may still not help.

rules.name: estimate_noise_before_trusting_deltas
rules.context: When the effect size of a change is similar to or smaller than suspected run-to-run variance (e.g., identical or near-identical re-runs show score fluctuations comparable to the delta from a change).
rules.action: Re-run identical code at least once to estimate submission noise. Only accept a change as real if its improvement exceeds 2× the observed run-to-run variance. Do not chase small regressions from cosmetic or no-op changes.
rules.exceptions: This consumes submission budget; the author in 13542132 never achieved actionable conclusions because the re-run strategy consumed budget without yielding clear signal.

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_bracketing_optimum
rules.context: When perturbations in both directions of a hyperparameter yield scores worse than or within noise of the current best, and 3+ attempts produce scores within a narrow band with no monotonic improvement trend.
rules.action: Stop tuning that parameter. Accept the best configuration found and move to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., feature engineering, model architecture, adding ensemble members) rather than continuing to permute the same parameter.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_consistent_regression
rules.context: When 3+ submitted attempts along the same lever (e.g., checkpoint swaps, weight variants, architecture changes) all regress from the baseline without any improvement.
rules.action: Stop the sweep and change strategy. Move to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., ensembling the best configurations, adding new models, or changing the lever entirely). Preserve the best-scoring configuration as a component for future use rather than discarding it.
rules.exceptions: 15082684 author ran 11 swaps instead of stopping at 3, suggesting some practitioners over-explore. The rule recommends stopping sooner.

rules.name: stop_meta_learner_tuning_pivot_to_base_models
rules.context: When 2-3 iterations of meta-learner or stacking combiner hyperparameter tuning fail to exceed the best score achieved with default or simple settings.
rules.action: Stop tuning the meta-learner and instead add new diverse base models to the ensemble. The marginal value of meta-learner hyperparameters is small compared to adding an uncorrelated base prediction.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: do_not_greedily_revert_small_regressions_in_noisy_lb
rules.context: When the leaderboard metric is noisy (few public test rows, or observed run-to-run variance is high) and a regression from a change is small (within the noise margin).
rules.action: Do not immediately revert a small regression. Continue the sweep to cover all candidate configurations. After the full sweep, select the best-scoring configuration rather than greedily reverting each individual regression. This avoids being misled by noise on single submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sweep_full_range_then_confirm_under_noise
rules.context: When leaderboard scores are noisy and you need to find the best value of a single scalar hyperparameter on a bounded interval.
rules.action: Sweep the full plausible range at a fixed step size rather than greedily hill-climbing, because noisy feedback can mislead greedy search. After the sweep, return to the best-performing value and re-confirm it. Hold all other parameters fixed during the sweep to avoid confounding.
rules.exceptions: 55987255 author confounded the signal by changing n_estimators simultaneously with blend weight.

rules.name: change_one_variable_at_a_time_when_effects_small
rules.context: When the expected effect size of each change is small (differences ~0.001 or less) and you want to explore multiple hyperparameters.
rules.action: After bracketing an optimum on one hyperparameter, revert it to the best-known value and change only the second hyperparameter. Never change two hyperparameters simultaneously when the expected effect size is small, because a regression cannot be attributed. If you do change two and regress, revert both to the last-known-good state before continuing.
rules.exceptions: 73671444 used forward-exploration instead of bisecting, which is faster when many untested model variants are queued but risks missing a valuable removed component.

rules.name: ablate_joint_changes_to_isolate_contributions
rules.context: When you change two or more variables at once and see a large improvement, and each submission is cheap enough to test individual reversions.
rules.action: Revert one variable back to its previous value while keeping the other fixed. If the score stays the same or improves, the reverted variable's new value was unnecessary or harmful. Repeat for the other variable. This isolates contributions with minimal submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: include_both_variants_when_swap_regresses
rules.context: When replacing component A with component B in an ensemble causes a regression, suggesting the removed component had unique predictive value.
rules.action: Include both A and B in the ensemble instead of choosing one. A regression from swapping suggests the components are complementary. If the combined ensemble beats both individual variants, keep it; otherwise revert to the better single variant.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sweep_individual_models_before_blending
rules.context: When you have multiple trained checkpoints or model variants with unknown relative LB performance and plan to build an ensemble.
rules.action: Submit each variant individually to the leaderboard first to establish per-variant scores. Do not stop early based on a bad result—complete the full sweep when variant count is small (≤5-8). Then use the collected LB scores to guide ensemble composition and weights. Only after identifying the best single recipe, scale up by adding folds/seeds from that recipe.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: move_on_after_quick_win_from_weight_tuning
rules.context: When a small adjustment to blend weights yields a new best score but the gain is modest and the weight space has limited remaining search space.
rules.action: After a quick win from blend weight tuning, move on to exploring new model components, architectures, or features rather than exhaustively searching the weight space. The marginal gain from fine-tuning weights among a few models is small compared to adding a genuinely complementary model.
rules.exceptions: 18423958 author's subsequent model explorations (DistilBERT) performed worse, suggesting sometimes sticking with weight tuning is safer.

rules.name: use_unsubmitted_runs_to_narrow_search
rules.context: When exploring a continuous parameter space and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Use local validation or unsubmitted runs to narrow the search space cheaply. Only submit when you have converged on a promising region or want to verify a candidate. After a score drop, reverse direction and try multiple candidate values without submitting before spending another submission.
rules.exceptions: 53747598 found that CV-guided selection did not transfer to LB for blend weights, so local validation may mislead for post-processing parameters.

rules.name: fix_infrastructure_before_judging_variable
rules.context: When a run fails or produces suspicious/broken output after changing an experimental variable (e.g., checkpoint, config).
rules.action: First check whether the failure is due to infrastructure issues (config paths, argument mismatches, data loading) rather than the variable itself. Fix the infrastructure, then re-submit. Do not count the failed run as evidence against the experimental variable.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_confounded_changes_before_continuing
rules.context: A submission regresses sharply after changing two or more variables simultaneously (e.g., backbone + resolution, checkpoint + preprocessing, architecture + data split).
rules.action: Revert entirely to the last known-good configuration. Then re-explore by changing only one variable at a time, submitting after each change. Do not attempt to salvage the new combination or fix individual parameters within the failed bundle.
rules.exceptions: 13577502:e3#2 notes the revert was partial (different dropout/augmentation), not clean. 7670859:e5#3 suggests an alternative: vary non-data changes first while holding data fixed, then revert data if needed.

rules.name: isolate_factors_after_multi_variable_improvement
rules.context: A combined change of two or more factors produced a score improvement, but it is unclear which factor contributed.
rules.action: In subsequent iterations, change only one factor at a time: partially revert one factor while keeping the other, then submit. Use the resulting score change as evidence for which factor to keep. Do not change multiple factors simultaneously again in the next step.
rules.exceptions: 7253130:e5#1 notes the author didn't do a clean single-variable ablation. 7018718:e9#1 notes the author sometimes still changed two factors at once.

rules.name: abandon_idea_after_consistent_underperformance
rules.context: A new idea (feature, architecture component, model variant) has been tried in 3+ meaningfully different configurations and none matches or exceeds the baseline on both CV and LB.
rules.action: Abandon the direction entirely. Revert to the prior best configuration and invest effort in a structurally different lever (e.g., different feature family, different model architecture). Do not continue micro-tuning the underperforming idea.
rules.exceptions: 27836972:e9#2 notes that CV scores close to the best may justify a bit more exploration. 55621328:e16#3 notes one large-model variant came close, but the author correctly prioritized the more reliable path.

rules.name: pivot_after_bracket_confirms_local_optimum
rules.context: A 3-point bracket sweep (lower, current, higher) of a single hyperparameter or knob confirms the current value is a local optimum, with both directions yielding worse scores.
rules.action: Accept the current parameter value and pivot to a qualitatively different lever (new features, different model family, ensembling). Do not continue refining the same parameter with smaller step sizes unless score differences are within leaderboard noise.
rules.exceptions: 55431616:e4#2 notes the author combined the revert with new features rather than testing independently.

rules.name: ensemble_sweep_one_member_at_a_time
rules.context: You have a small set of candidate models or checkpoints for an ensemble and want to find the best combination using leaderboard feedback.
rules.action: Establish a baseline blend. Then vary one dimension at a time: add/remove a single member, or change one weight. When removing a component worsens the score, keep it. When adding members, continue until gains plateau. Do not change multiple members or weights simultaneously. Stop after all candidates are tested or consecutive improvements drop below noise level.
rules.exceptions: 15173072:e5#1 notes the author did change multiple things simultaneously in several steps, undermining attribution.

rules.name: enumerate_then_ensemble_small_option_sets
rules.context: The option space is small enough to enumerate completely (e.g., <10 checkpoints or model variants) and individual options show small, noisy score differences on the leaderboard.
rules.action: Submit each option once to get a rough ranking. If score differences between top options are small relative to noise, stop trying to pick a single winner and instead ensemble the top 2-3 candidates. Do not re-test the same option expecting different results unless another variable has changed.
rules.exceptions: 7606235:e2#2 notes the author re-tested options and got different scores, suggesting uncontrolled variables in the pipeline.

rules.name: blend_weight_tuning_stop_criterion
rules.context: You are tuning continuous blend weights for a small ensemble (2-4 models) using leaderboard feedback, and the leaderboard may be noisy.
rules.action: Try 3-5 perturbations around the current best weights in steps of 0.05-0.15. If the first perturbation worsens, move in the opposite direction. If after ~4 attempts none beats the baseline, stop—the weights are near-optimal. On very noisy leaderboards (few evaluation rows), make only 2-3 structurally distinct attempts rather than fine-grained sweeps.
rules.exceptions: 77386286:e2#1 notes the author did not follow a strictly systematic grid and some jumps were large.

rules.name: revert_immediately_on_clear_single_variable_regression
rules.context: A single-variable change (e.g., switching regularization type, applying a transformation universally) produces a score drop clearly larger than typical noise.
rules.action: Immediately revert the change in the next iteration. Redirect effort to tuning the previously better variant's hyperparameters or to a different lever entirely. Do not spend multiple iterations trying to rescue the clearly inferior variant.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: never_bundle_cleanup_with_experimental_revert
rules.context: You want to revert an unsuccessful experimental change and also clean up dead code or remove an inference block in the same submission.
rules.action: Submit the experimental revert alone first to confirm the score impact. Only then clean up dead code in a separate submission. Bundling functional changes with refactoring makes regressions unattributable.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: add_resource_heavy_member_by_swap_then_restore
rules.context: Adding a large new model to an already-large ensemble may exceed resource limits or dilute quality, and some existing members may be redundant.
rules.action: First add the new member while disabling several existing members to create headroom. Submit to verify the new member works. Then re-enable disabled members one at a time, submitting after each, to find the best subset. Keep the configuration that achieved the best score.
rules.exceptions: 18523075:e6#1 notes the author did not revert a regression, prioritizing exhaustive coverage over strict greedy improvement.

rules.name: stop_gbdt_hyperparam_tuning_at_plateau
rules.context: GBDT hyperparameter tuning has been attempted and scores have plateaued (no improvement after one or two adjustment rounds), whether after extensive feature engineering or after a hyperparameter sweep.
rules.action: Make at most one final micro-adjustment to confirm the plateau. If no improvement, stop tuning hyperparameters and switch to a different lever (e.g., new features, model architecture, or ensembling). Continuing to search the same hyperparameter space yields diminishing or negative returns.
rules.exceptions: When feature engineering has plateaued but hyperparameters have never been tuned (as in 27836972), an initial substantial change (e.g., increasing tree depth, lowering learning rate, adding regularization) can still yield a meaningful gain before the hyperparameter plateau sets in.

rules.name: fold_count_increase_diminishing_returns
rules.context: When tuning the number of CV folds on a moderately-sized dataset (roughly 6K–17K samples) and you already have a working fold count that produces good scores.
rules.action: Increase fold count modestly (e.g., 5→10 or 10→15) rather than aggressively (e.g., 15→20 or 5→30). If increasing folds causes leaderboard regression on two or more attempts, revert to the lower count. Excessively high fold counts can produce validation sets too small for reliable metric estimation and noisier individual models that hurt the ensemble. On very small datasets, moderate increases help by giving more training data per fold.
rules.exceptions: On very small datasets (~6K), larger fold increases (e.g., 10→15) can yield meaningful gains because marginal training examples matter more (7253130:e5#2). The optimal fold count is dataset- and metric-dependent.

rules.name: verify_cv_locally_before_submitting
rules.context: When changing CV infrastructure (fold count, model family, or averaging logic) in a competition pipeline.
rules.action: Run a non-submitted validation pass to confirm local CV scores are reasonable before submitting, to avoid wasting submission quota on infrastructure bugs. When changing fold count, update all downstream averaging code to match the new count. When increasing folds substantially, confirm that OOF metrics stabilize before committing to the new configuration.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: probe_class_reweighting_carefully_for_imbalanced_targets
rules.context: Binary or ordinal classification with class imbalance, where the competition metric weights classes asymmetrically or is rank-sensitive (e.g., normalized Gini, QWK), and a GBDT or AutoML model is already performing well.
rules.action: Probe class/sample reweighting in isolation (one parameter at a time). For GBDT, sweep scale_pos_weight exponent in small steps and submit each. If the custom metric already guides model selection or the model's native ranking ability handles the asymmetry, revert weights when OOF/LB does not improve. Avoid naive oversampling (e.g., SMOTE) for ordinal targets—prefer threshold optimization or loss-based weighting instead.
rules.exceptions: For GBDT scale_pos_weight, sweeping the exponent did yield improvement in one case (27656049), so the revert-if-no-gain guidance mainly applies when the metric is already used for model selection (27502740) or when the reweighting method doesn't respect target structure (59253662:SMOTE on ordinal).

rules.name: linear_meta_learner_for_stacking
rules.context: When stacking multiple base model predictions (OOF) as meta-features and the meta-feature space is low-dimensional (handful to ~20 base model predictions), especially with limited training data.
rules.action: Start with a simple linear meta-learner (Ridge regression or LinearRegression) rather than nonlinear alternatives. Ridge is preferred over Lasso when you already perform explicit feature elimination. If a nonlinear meta-learner (e.g., RBF SVR) does not improve OOF score, revert to the linear model rather than tuning kernel hyperparameters.
rules.exceptions: Ridge stacking alone may not beat well-tuned weighted averaging until combined with iterative feature elimination (73937748:e11#1). On very small datasets, even linear models may need regularization tuning.

rules.name: curate_base_model_subset_for_meta_learner
rules.context: When a stacking meta-learner has access to many base-model OOF predictions of varying quality, and some may be noisy or redundant.
rules.action: Curate a subset of base-model predictions rather than passing all to the meta-learner. Use iterative feature elimination: drop each base model one at a time and keep the removal if OOF score improves. Validate by toggling the filter off; if LB drops, keep the filter. Weak or redundant members add noise the meta-learner may not fully ignore.
rules.exceptions: Benefit may be marginal (~0.001 in 75924487:e4#2); the meta-learner switch alone was insufficient without elimination in 73937748:e11#1.

rules.name: scale_iterations_inversely_with_learning_rate
rules.context: When reducing the learning rate of a gradient boosting model that uses early stopping, and the maximum number of boosting rounds (n_estimators) or early_stopping_rounds have not been proportionally adjusted.
rules.action: Increase n_estimators by at least the inverse ratio of the learning rate reduction (e.g., halving LR → at least double n_estimators). Also increase early_stopping_rounds to allow enough rounds for convergence at the lower LR. When increasing LR substantially, consider increasing max_depth by 1 to give more capacity per round; when decreasing LR, reduce depth back. Verify via validation curves that the model has converged before submitting.
rules.exceptions: 60759531:e2#2 shows that even with increased n_estimators, simultaneous changes to other settings (e.g., random_state, regularization) can confound the signal, so avoid changing learning rate and regularization simultaneously.

rules.name: revert_quickly_if_optimizer_or_head_change_regresses
rules.context: When switching to a new optimizer or re-tuning head hyperparameters (dropout, LR) after a significant architectural or loss-function change in a neural network, and the first probe submission shows regression.
rules.action: Probe the change in a single submission. If it regresses, revert immediately and instead re-tune the original optimizer's or head's hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, dropout) rather than spending time tuning the new configuration. Isolate each variable by reverting one at a time to determine which change actually helped.
rules.exceptions: Attribution can be confounded when multiple changes are bundled (e.g., bug fixes, scheduler changes alongside optimizer swap), so ensure only one variable changes per probe.

rules.name: ensemble_membership_selection_by_incremental_swap
rules.context: You have multiple trained model variants/checkpoints and want to find the best ensemble combination, with limited submission budget or noisy leaderboard signal.
rules.action: Evaluate candidate models individually first to establish standalone quality. Then build the ensemble incrementally: add or swap one member at a time, submit, and compare. If the score improves, keep the change; if it regresses, revert that member and try a different candidate. When uniform averaging dilutes a strong model, switch to weighted blending. Stop when consecutive swaps regress or candidates are exhausted.
rules.exceptions: 60264017: author did not always fully revert before trying the next swap, suggesting partial revert plus forward exploration can also work. 52860091: a weak model can still help in ensemble (v0+v1 beat both alone), but this doesn't always hold (v0+v2 was worse than v2 alone).

rules.name: revert_and_redirect_on_regression
rules.context: A new configuration (ensemble member swap, augmentation strategy, or lever variant) causes a leaderboard regression, and you have a known-good prior configuration.
rules.action: Do not persist with the regressing configuration. Revert to the last known-good state. Try a different candidate or approach in the next submission. If two consecutive attempts from the same lever regress, abandon that lever and switch to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., new model family, different blending method, or diagnostic investigation).
rules.exceptions: 60264017: after second regression the author moved to a new approach rather than reverting and trying another swap, suggesting candidate exhaustion can also trigger stopping. 15372370: author did not submit the intermediate revert, so incremental revert wasn't fully LB-validated.

rules.name: isolate_regression_by_ablation
rules.context: Combining components (models in ensemble, or multiple simultaneous changes) causes a significant score regression compared to individual components or the prior baseline.
rules.action: Immediately isolate by running each component alone to confirm individual quality. Check merging/integration code for bugs (e.g., incorrect concatenation, misaligned predictions). Only after confirming components work individually and integration logic is correct, re-test the combination. For multi-component changes, remove the most aggressive/novel component first, test, then continue removing until regression source is identified.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: batch_infrastructure_changes_before_submitting
rules.context: A new approach requires coordinated changes across multiple pipeline components, and intermediate states are broken or not meaningful to evaluate.
rules.action: Batch all prerequisite infrastructure changes without submitting. Use intermediate versions to inspect outputs (e.g., display dataframe heads, list directories, check shapes) to confirm correctness locally. Only submit once the complete pipeline is assembled and verified end-to-end. This avoids wasting submission quota on uninformative scores.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: test_candidate_model_solo_then_in_blend
rules.context: You have a new candidate model and an existing ensemble of proven models, and want to evaluate whether the candidate adds value.
rules.action: First test the candidate model solo (or with minimal blending) to gauge standalone quality. Then add it to the existing blend and compare. A weak solo model may still contribute diversity, so do not discard based on solo score alone—judge by the final blend score. If adding it worsens the blend despite decent solo quality, try weighted blending before discarding.
rules.exceptions: 52860091: v0+v2 was worse than v2 alone despite v0 being decent solo, showing that diversity contribution is not guaranteed.

rules.name: simplify_model_when_small_data_or_invariant_model
rules.context: When model complexity (extra preprocessing layers, larger hidden layers, or multi-layer stacking heads) is not yielding performance gains, and either (a) the training set is small (<10K rows) suggesting overfitting risk, or (b) the model family is inherently invariant to the removed steps (e.g., tree models handle missingness and are scale-invariant).
rules.action: Simplify the pipeline: remove unnecessary preprocessing (scaling, imputation, outlier removal) for invariant models; reduce stacking heads to simple weighted averages for small datasets; shrink MLP depth/width when capacity increases show no gain. Verify on LB that simplification does not hurt. If it degrades, revert. Change only one component at a time to correctly attribute effects.
rules.exceptions: 28093671:e8#3 notes that post-aggregation cleanup (imputation of NaN aggregates) may still be needed even when raw-feature imputation is removed. 18550705:e5#2 warns that changing multiple components simultaneously (e.g., stacking head and ensemble membership) prevents proper attribution of any degradation.

rules.name: hierarchical_blending_for_correlated_models
rules.context: When ensembling multiple model predictions where some sources are correlated (same architecture, similar training, or meta-learner trained on base model outputs) and others are more independent.
rules.action: Group correlated predictors into sub-averages first, then combine sub-group means at a second level using a separate weighted average. This prevents correlated models from dominating. Give groups with more diverse/independent predictions slightly higher weight. Do not simply append meta-learner predictions into the same flat averaging pool as base models.
rules.exceptions: When public LB feedback is very noisy (e.g., 7 rows), further refinement within the hierarchical scheme may regress (18837555:e5#1). Optimal structure may require more than two levels when additional diverse components are added (17616127:e10#2).

rules.name: alternative_averaging_space_for_ensemble
rules.context: When probability-based ensemble averaging has plateaued or component models have different calibration scales, and raw logits or rank information is available.
rules.action: Try averaging in an alternative space: either convert predictions to ranks before weighted averaging (to normalize calibration differences), or average raw logits before applying softmax (to preserve confidence magnitudes). Keep existing blend weights initially to isolate the effect of the space change, then re-tune weights under the new method if it matches or beats the baseline.
rules.exceptions: Improvements may be modest and confounded with simultaneous weight changes (53747598:e4#1). Rank-based averaging may only tie probability-based until weights are re-tuned (15164527:e4#2).

rules.name: single_probe_before_ensemble_integration
rules.context: A new model or new model artifacts are available and their standalone quality is unknown, and you want to decide whether to add them to an existing ensemble or stacking pipeline.
rules.action: Test the new component in isolation first (standalone score or single-change submission). If standalone performance is far worse than existing components, do not integrate. If integrated as a single probe and LB regresses or fails to improve, abandon the addition quickly rather than tuning integration details. Limit to at most two submissions on this binary include/exclude test.
rules.exceptions: A weak standalone model can still help through diversity (17616127 counter_evidence), so this heuristic may discard useful diverse members. Also, confounded changes (59253662) can mask the true signal.

rules.name: ablate_after_bundled_regression
rules.context: Multiple changes were bundled in one commit/submission and the leaderboard score regressed, making it unclear which change caused the drop.
rules.action: Remove or modify the most suspicious single component first and resubmit. If score partially recovers, that component was harmful. If it does not fully recover, suspect other concurrent changes. After at most two diagnostic submissions, if baseline is not recovered, revert all bundled changes to restore the known-good baseline and pursue a different lever entirely.
rules.exceptions: When the regression is tiny (within noise), it may not be worth diagnosing at all—just move on (59253662:e6#2). Partial recovery may indicate multiple interacting causes (77276039:e4#2).

rules.name: limit_submissions_on_failed_external_data_or_component
rules.context: Adding external data or a new component (external model predictions, auxiliary dataset) shows regression or no improvement after initial submissions, and alternative levers exist.
rules.action: Allow at most two submission attempts with variations (e.g., different filtering, different integration). If both fail to improve over baseline, revert all related changes and move to an orthogonal lever. Do not continue tuning the failed addition's parameters.
rules.exceptions: More sophisticated approaches (pseudo-labeling, careful filtering) might eventually help, so this rule trades potential gains for time efficiency (49576186 counter_evidence).

rules.name: incremental_changes_avoid_consecutive_failures
rules.context: Modifying an inference or training pipeline by adding multiple prediction calls, aggregation steps, or variable renames in a single edit.
rules.action: Make changes incrementally: first add prediction calls and verify they run, then add aggregation, then wire to submission. Do a find-and-replace check on all variable references before submitting. This avoids consecutive failed runs that waste submission budget.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: prune_weak_ensemble_members
rules.context: When an ensemble (stacking or weighted blend) includes a model whose OOF performance is noticeably worse than other members, or when adding a new model caused a score regression.
rules.action: Remove the weakest model entirely rather than relying on the optimizer/stacker to downweight it. Re-run the ensemble and verify on LB. Even with optimized weights, a weak member can inject noise the optimizer cannot fully suppress. If removal improves the score, continue pruning the next weakest; if it worsens, restore and try removing a different member.
rules.exceptions: In larger ensembles or with highly diverse architectures, even weaker members can help through diversity (18757376 notes this for larger data). Also, ordering of removals matters—removing the wrong member first can worsen the score (18550705 counter_evidence).

rules.name: swap_variants_in_fixed_ensemble_slot
rules.context: When you have multiple checkpoint variants or training configurations of the same base architecture (e.g., different training procedures, different fine-tuning configs) and need to choose one for an ensemble slot.
rules.action: Try each variant in the same ensemble slot while keeping all other members fixed. Submit each configuration and keep the variant that yields the best LB score. This is higher-signal than including both variants, which may introduce correlated noise. Vary one factor at a time to avoid confounding.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: select_dominant_member_via_lb_verification
rules.context: When two strong models alternate as the top-weighted or dominant member across local CV runs, and you cannot resolve which is better from CV alone.
rules.action: Test each candidate as the dominant ensemble member with its best companion weights, submit both configurations, and keep the one with higher LB. Do not rely solely on CV when the candidates are close—LB verification breaks the tie. If the best pre-episode configuration used the other candidate, the advantage may be configuration-dependent.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is limited, use OOF correlation analysis to pre-filter before spending submissions (75924487).

rules.name: verify_ensemble_integrity_before_modifying
rules.context: You have a large ensemble at a known best score and want to either prune members or refactor the pipeline. Individual components may score worse than the ensemble.
rules.action: Before making algorithmic changes, verify the current ensemble reproduces the baseline score. When pruning, remove members in small batches and submit; if score worsens, reverse rather than pruning further. When refactoring infrastructure, submit to confirm no regression before proceeding to new experiments. Keep pruning/refactoring and experimentation in separate submissions.
rules.exceptions: When the public LB has very few samples (e.g., ~7 rows), even small-batch pruning results are noisy and hard to attribute; one-at-a-time removal is more informative but costlier in submissions.

rules.name: add_diverse_backbone_and_rebalance_weights
rules.context: You have a working multi-model ensemble of pretrained transformer backbones and want to improve it further, especially when existing members share similar architecture families or the score has plateaued.
rules.action: Add a new member from a different architecture family or training run. Start with a modest initial blend weight (e.g., 0.1 or roughly uniform). Submit to confirm it doesn't hurt. Then re-optimize blend weights using OOF predictions, down-weighting members that contribute least. If the new member yields only marginal or no improvement, consider replacing the weakest existing member with a stronger backbone rather than continuing to tune weights.
rules.exceptions: Gains from backbone diversity can be modest (e.g., 0.00079 RMSE or flat). In 18851026, the author later replaced the diverse backbone (T5) with more variants of the dominant family (RoBERTa), suggesting backbone diversity alone isn't always decisive. In 18350823, adding a fourth member with modest weight produced essentially no improvement.

rules.name: isolate_changes_after_regression
rules.context: A submission that bundled multiple changes (e.g., new checkpoints across all folds, or multiple hyperparameter changes at once) caused a score regression, and you cannot attribute the cause.
rules.action: Revert to the last known-good configuration, then re-apply changes one at a time with a submission after each to isolate which factor caused the regression. For checkpoint swaps: use per-fold CV to identify which folds improved and construct a mixed list. For hyperparameters: fix all but one variable and sweep it before moving to the next. Only combine changes once each is validated individually.
rules.exceptions: Per-fold cherry-picking across checkpoint sources may introduce distribution mismatch (18426209 counter_evidence: mixed selection still didn't beat original).

rules.name: resubmit_identical_to_estimate_noise
rules.context: Leaderboard score differences between configurations are small (comparable to or smaller than suspected evaluation noise), making single-submission comparisons unreliable.
rules.action: Submit the same unchanged notebook multiple times to estimate the leaderboard noise floor. If noise is ~0.005-0.01, compare configurations using median or best-of-N scores across multiple runs rather than single submissions. Only declare a configuration better when the gap exceeds the observed noise range. For quick checks, one re-submission suffices; for close calls, use 5-8 runs.
rules.exceptions: Consumes submission slots; may degenerate into cherry-picking the best random score rather than genuine noise estimation (50376011 counter_evidence).

rules.name: evaluate_checkpoints_individually_then_combine
rules.context: Multiple trained checkpoint sets (from different training runs, architectures, or sources) are available, and swapping checkpoints in the inference pipeline is cheap (e.g., a path change).
rules.action: Evaluate each checkpoint set individually via separate submissions. Discard any set that causes a large regression. Then combine the top-performing sets into one ensemble. If the combined result doesn't beat the individual best or the pre-existing baseline, revert to the previous best. Prioritize swapping to a clearly superior checkpoint before tuning inference-time settings around it.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: toggle_transform_in_isolation_before_fixing
rules.context: A prediction transform (e.g., sqrt, power transform) or calibration step gave mixed or confounded signals about whether it helps, because other changes were made simultaneously.
rules.action: Test the transform in isolation by toggling it on/off with all other settings held constant. If removing it hurts, restore it immediately and treat it as a fixed component for subsequent tuning. Do not re-test unless the ensemble composition changes substantially. Note that rank-based averaging may implicitly replace calibration transforms.
rules.exceptions: When switching to rank-based averaging, calibration transforms become redundant since ranks replace raw probabilities (15164527 counter_evidence).

rules.name: explicit_deterministic_checkpoint_loading
rules.context: When loading model checkpoints for inference or ensembling, and the loading mechanism involves implicit discovery (e.g., glob) or silent fallback (e.g., pretrained=True with strict=False), producing unpredictable or mixed weight states.
rules.action: Make checkpoint loading explicit and deterministic: use hard-coded file paths (annotated with fold/score metadata) instead of glob discovery, set pretrained=False when loading fine-tuned checkpoints, and use strict=True in load_state_dict. Fix model definition mismatches rather than silently skipping keys.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: stop_same_lever_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: 3-4 consecutive submissions tuning the same lever (e.g., blend weights, augmentation strength, a single hyperparameter) all regress from the known best score, with no upward trend.
rules.action: Stop tuning that lever and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., from weight tuning to adding a new model, from augmentation to loss function). The consecutive regressions signal the current lever is not the binding constraint. If you must continue, try at most one more alternative configuration before abandoning the lever entirely.
rules.exceptions: 13542132:e3#1 shows the author tried one more step after 3 regressions before stopping, suggesting the threshold may be 4 rather than 3 in some cases. 58130512:e30#1 shows the author did NOT follow this rule and suffered 5 consecutive regressions.

rules.name: revert_to_best_before_trying_new_direction
rules.context: A submission regresses from the known best score, and you want to try a different configuration next.
rules.action: Revert to the exact last-best configuration before trying a different knob or direction. Do not chain changes on top of a regressed configuration. If you change multiple knobs simultaneously and regress, you cannot isolate which change hurt. Change only one knob per submission to maintain attribution.
rules.exceptions: 18426209:e7#1 shows the author did NOT revert to the known-best 0.5/0.5 after regression, instead trying a different blend—deviating from strict revert-on-regression. 58130512:e30#1 shows the author changed multiple knobs per step and never reverted, resulting in inability to isolate causes.

rules.name: prefer_fixed_weights_on_noisy_leaderboard
rules.context: The public leaderboard is computed on very few samples (e.g., <10 rows), making single-submission score comparisons unreliable, and you are considering data-adaptive or conditional blending logic.
rules.action: Prefer fixed blend weights over data-adaptive conditional logic. If a conditional strategy does not clearly beat the simple fixed-weight version, revert to fixed weights immediately. On noisy leaderboards, try one alternative configuration after a regression before concluding the direction is unproductive, but do not iterate extensively on conditional approaches.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: add_diverse_model_when_weight_tuning_plateaus
rules.context: Blend-weight tuning across existing models has failed to improve the score after 3-4 attempts, and the ensemble score is plateaued.
rules.action: Stop tuning weights and instead add a new, architecturally diverse model to the ensemble. Weight tuning has diminishing returns when component predictions are too correlated. Before submitting the new model's ensemble, verify it doesn't break the pipeline via local CV. Only submit after confirming CV is reasonable.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: bisect_continuous_hyperparam_near_optimum
rules.context: You are sweeping a continuous hyperparameter (e.g., blend weight, regularization), large steps cause regressions, and moderate steps yield small gains, suggesting the optimum is nearby.
rules.action: Start with coarse steps to identify the improvement direction. When a step causes regression, reverse direction and halve the step size. When two consecutive submissions differ by less than noise, declare the optimum bracketed and stop sweeping that parameter. Move to a qualitatively different lever.
rules.exceptions: 18426209:e7#1 shows the author did not strictly follow bisection—after regression at 0.65/0.35, they tried adding a third model rather than reversing direction on the same two-model weight.

rules.name: fix_pipeline_bugs_before_continuing_sweep
rules.context: During an ensemble tuning sweep, a model that should be strong performs unexpectedly poorly, or you discover a data/model mismatch (e.g., shape mismatch, dead code, preprocessing inconsistency).
rules.action: Stop the weight search. Fix the bug, then re-run the best-known ensemble configuration to get a clean baseline before further tuning. Do not continue optimizing weights on top of a buggy pipeline.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: sweep_blend_weights_one_knob_at_a_time
rules.context: You have 2+ pretrained models combined via blend weights, and you are tuning weights using leaderboard or CV feedback.
rules.action: Change only one knob (blend weight) per submission so score changes can be attributed. Sweep in coarse steps (~0.05–0.1) first, then refine with finer increments (~0.01) around the best value. Do not simultaneously change blend weights and model hyperparameters or other corrections (e.g., additive bias). If single-knob sweeps show no signal after a few steps, the models may be too correlated for weight tuning to help.
rules.exceptions: In 55591012:e12#2 the author sometimes changed blend weights and reg_alpha simultaneously, slowing attribution. In 7823861:e7#2, weight tuning yielded no improvement, suggesting effort should shift to model diversity.

rules.name: weight_stronger_model_higher_in_initial_blend
rules.context: You have multiple models with known individual scores (from CV or solo LB submissions) and need to set initial blend weights.
rules.action: Assign higher initial weight (e.g., 70–80%) to the model with the best solo score. Test each new model solo first to establish standalone quality. Then combine, using solo scores to inform weight allocation. Start from this informed prior and sweep outward rather than starting from equal weights. Exception: when models have very similar CV scores from the same architecture, start with equal weights instead.
rules.exceptions: 15173072:e5#3 shows that when models have similar CV scores and the same architecture, equal weighting is preferred and unequal weights don't help.

rules.name: prefer_balanced_weights_over_cv_extreme_weights
rules.context: CV-optimal blend weights heavily downweight or nearly zero out one model, but LB feedback suggests more balanced weights perform better.
rules.action: Prefer weights closer to uniform or to the last LB-validated configuration rather than aggressively trusting CV. Extreme weight skew (nearly zeroing a model) risks overfitting to CV folds and losing diversity that helps on unseen data. When CV and LB disagree, use the more balanced weighting as default.
rules.exceptions: Evidence is limited; when CV is highly reliable (many folds, large dataset), trusting CV may be correct.

rules.name: diminishing_returns_from_adding_models_without_cv_weight_optimization
rules.context: You are adding a third or fourth model to an existing blend and tuning weights via leaderboard submissions without reliable local CV for weight optimization.
rules.action: Be cautious: adding more models with coarse LB-based weight tuning often yields diminishing or negative returns compared to a simpler 2-model blend. Before adding models, verify each new model improves the blend in local CV. If no reliable CV exists, test the new model solo first, then try a simple equal-weight addition. If the expanded blend doesn't beat the simpler one, revert.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: allow_negative_weights_when_positive_blend_underperforms
rules.context: An Optuna-tuned or grid-searched weighted ensemble with positive-only normalized weights underperforms a Ridge or linear meta-learner that can assign negative/unnormalized coefficients.
rules.action: Expand the weight search range to include negative values (e.g., [-1, 1]) and remove the sum-to-one normalization constraint. This makes the blend more expressive, approaching a linear meta-learner. If this still underperforms Ridge, the meta-learner's regularization is providing additional value beyond signed weights.
rules.exceptions: In 73937748:e16#2, even negative weights didn't match Ridge stacking, suggesting regularization matters beyond weight sign flexibility.

rules.name: ensemble_blend_weights_update_strategy
rules.context: When blending multiple diverse models (different architectures or different model versions) and updating the ensemble composition by adding or swapping a component model.
rules.action: If the new component is architecturally diverse or substantially different, retune blend weights jointly across all components, weighting stronger standalone models more heavily. If the swap is a minor incremental upgrade of an existing component, first try keeping blend coefficients fixed—only retune if the score does not improve. Adding a third diverse model can beat a two-model blend even if individually weaker.
rules.exceptions: Marginal gains from adding weaker diverse models may be negligible (e.g., 0.0004 improvement); the fixed-coefficient strategy for incremental upgrades was only validated in one case and may not generalize.

rules.name: keep_inference_behavior_consistent_with_training
rules.context: During inference, adaptive or dynamic settings (e.g., dropout rate, dynamic input shapes) differ from what was used at training time, and score improvements are absent or inconsistent.
rules.action: Revert inference-time settings to match training-time configuration. Disable dynamic/adaptive features (dropout, dynamic shapes, adaptive batching) during inference. If deterministic inference (e.g., dropout=0) doesn't help, stop searching other inference-time variations of that setting — the lever is unproductive.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: advanced_pooling_for_small_text_regression
rules.context: When fine-tuning a pretrained transformer (e.g., RoBERTa) for regression on a small text dataset (~2800 samples) and the current model uses simple CLS or mean pooling.
rules.action: Experiment with richer pooling strategies: attention-based pooling over last hidden states, or weighted hidden-layer pooling (initialize layer weights as zeros for uniform weighting after softmax, concatenate mean-pooled and max-pooled representations). Validate via CV before submitting. Note that these changes alone on a single model may not beat a diverse ensemble, and combining with layer reinitialization can regress if layers don't converge—revert reinitialization before discarding the pooling change.
rules.exceptions: Combined pooling + layer reinitialization regressed on LB in one case (18757376:e5#2). A single improved-pooling model did not beat a multi-variant ensemble (17371717:e3#2), suggesting architectural improvements to one model may not substitute for model diversity.

rules.name: match_pooling_to_checkpoint_at_inference
rules.context: When you have multiple trained checkpoints that were trained with different architectural variants (e.g., mean+max pooling vs. mean-only pooling) and need to select the best inference configuration.
rules.action: Ensure the pooling strategy at inference matches the one used during training for each checkpoint. Sweep all valid (pooling, checkpoint) combinations and compare LB scores. If neither variant consistently wins, pick the one with the best single result and refine checkpoint choice within that variant. Do not mix a checkpoint trained with one pooling type with a different pooling type at inference.
rules.exceptions: Sweeping a small number of combinations may be incomplete; the best combination may require a checkpoint not yet available (17371717:e13#1).

rules.name: revert_to_baseline_on_regression
rules.context: A hyperparameter change or ensemble weight change causes a score regression from a known-good baseline, and multiple parameters were changed simultaneously making it unclear which caused the drop.
rules.action: Fully revert to the exact known-good baseline configuration before trying the next change. Never stack untested changes on top of a regression. Test one parameter (or one component) at a time against the baseline to isolate effects. If partial rollback is attempted, keep only 1-2 changes you have strongest reason to believe are beneficial.
rules.exceptions: In 60759531, the author only partially reverted while changing other parameters simultaneously, which prevented isolation but did not completely block progress. In 77450317, the regression was due to stale component models rather than HP changes, so the fix was upgrading components rather than reverting HPs.

rules.name: fix_seed_during_manual_hp_sweep
rules.context: You are manually sweeping hyperparameters using leaderboard or CV scores as feedback, and training involves stochastic elements (random seeds, NN initialization, etc.).
rules.action: Hold the random seed fixed while varying hyperparameters so score changes can be attributed to the HP, not seed variance. Do not change random seeds simultaneously with other parameters. If you must assess seed robustness, do a seed-only run first to estimate variance before interpreting HP effects.
rules.exceptions: The author in 60759531 eventually reached a good score despite changing seeds throughout, so the confounding slowed but did not prevent progress.

rules.name: upgrade_components_when_blend_tuning_regresses
rules.context: Ensemble blend weight tuning has regressed or plateaued for 2-3 consecutive attempts, and the component model predictions have not been updated recently.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights on stale predictions. Instead, upgrade or add new diverse component models (retrained or improved versions). Then retune blend weights jointly with the new components. Verify with a submission before iterating further.
rules.exceptions: The stopping threshold is flexible—75145694 continued for 3 declining submissions past the peak rather than stopping at 2.

rules.name: confirm_multifactor_change_before_iterating
rules.context: You have made multiple simultaneous modifications (e.g., new model versions + new blend weights, or several HPs at once) and the notebook has stochastic elements.
rules.action: After a multi-factor change, re-run the notebook unchanged and submit to confirm the score before making further modifications. This separates the signal of the change from run-to-run variance. Only proceed to the next iteration after confirming improvement.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ensemble_seed_fold_averaging
rules.context: A trained model (neural network or transformer) scores well but predictions are noisy, and multiple checkpoints from different random seeds or CV folds are available without changing the training recipe.
rules.action: Average predictions across all available fold checkpoints first for a meaningful variance-reduction gain, then add additional seed/repeat runs incrementally. Sweep the repeat count upward in small increments while score improves; when a step regresses, treat the previous value as the optimum and stop. Do not change other hyperparameters simultaneously, as confounded changes make regressions uninterpretable.
rules.exceptions: Changing multiple knobs (e.g., architecture settings and repeat count) at once can cause large regressions that are hard to diagnose (77129691 v8→v9).

rules.name: discretize_predictions_to_match_target_levels
rules.context: Model outputs continuous predictions but ground-truth labels take only a few discrete values (e.g., crowd-rating averages, ordinal scores), and the metric is rank-based or ordinal (Spearman, QWK).
rules.action: Post-process predictions by snapping/rounding them to the known discrete target levels using optimized thresholds rather than naive uniform midpoints. Start with columns/targets that have the most discrete structure (binary or few-level). Expand one column at a time, validating via OOF metric. If a batch of changes causes regression, revert to the last known-good version rather than attempting incremental fixes.
