rules.exceptions: Not all target columns benefit equally from discretization; scaling all columns at once can hurt (7548275:e6#1 v24 regression). Aggressive intermediate binning or too many simultaneous threshold changes can cause large regressions (7823861:e5#1 v22→v23).

rules.name: pivot_architecture_when_incremental_tuning_plateaus
rules.context: You have been iterating on a single model architecture (swapping checkpoints, tuning preprocessing, or hyperparameters) and scores have plateaued or local CV improvements no longer translate to leaderboard gains.
rules.action: Stop incremental tuning of the current architecture. Instead, make a structural change: either port successful preprocessing/augmentation improvements to a different architecture variant, or redesign the model head (e.g., add attention mechanisms, multi-head outputs). Evaluate each architecture variant with the best-known preprocessing and select based on leaderboard feedback rather than local CV alone.
rules.exceptions: Both items have limited causal evidence—one infers the benefit from a single checkpoint comparison, the other from a post-episode pivot. The rule is strongest when multiple architecture options are readily available.

rules.name: match_inference_preprocessing_to_training
rules.context: When running inference with a trained checkpoint and the inference pipeline's preprocessing parameters (resolution, normalization, scaling, frequency cropping, etc.) may differ from what the model was trained with.
rules.action: Before tuning model architecture or ensembling, verify that all inference preprocessing exactly matches training: input resolution, normalization mean/std, spectrogram parameters (n_fft, win_length, hop_length, scaling), frequency crops, and any dataset-specific transforms. Fix all mismatches in one pass. If the training config is unknown, test first without extra preprocessing, then with it. Do not change preprocessing parameters at inference time unless the model was trained with those exact parameters; if experimenting, change only one parameter at a time and expect regressions from mismatches.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: revert_or_restore_after_catastrophic_infrastructure_regression
rules.context: An infrastructure or dependency refactoring (not a modeling change) causes a catastrophic score drop (>10% or near-random), and a single corrective attempt does not fully restore performance.
rules.action: Revert to the last known-good version immediately rather than continuing incremental patches. Diagnose the root cause offline before re-attempting the refactoring. If the drop was caused by intentional ablation for diagnostics, keep the pre-ablation code intact (commented out) so restoration is trivial, complete the diagnostic sweep, then restore in one step.
rules.exceptions: If the drop is from an intentional diagnostic ablation (not a real regression), do not panic-revert — complete the investigation first, then restore.

rules.name: systematic_inference_pipeline_debugging_on_near_random_score
rules.context: Leaderboard score is drastically lower than expected (near random) despite a model with strong training/CV metrics, indicating a pipeline bug rather than a weak model.
rules.action: Systematically check each inference pipeline stage: (1) correct checkpoint loaded, (2) model in eval mode, (3) correct input normalization, (4) no weight-loading conflicts (e.g., strict=False masking errors, pretrained flag overwriting checkpoint), (5) prediction value scaling matches submission format. Print raw prediction statistics (min, max, mean) and compare against sample submission ranges. Fix one thing per submission to isolate the cause.
rules.exceptions: AUC is theoretically scale-invariant, so prediction scaling fixes may indicate a platform-specific issue rather than a true scaling problem.

rules.name: fix_all_bugs_then_verify_end_to_end_before_submit
rules.context: Adapting or refactoring a notebook that has multiple correctness issues (variable name mismatches, dead code paths, indentation errors, missing dependencies).
rules.action: Fix all identified bugs in one pass, then immediately run the notebook end-to-end before submitting. After moving code out of conditional blocks, verify indentation matches the surrounding scope. After removing package dependencies, verify the model can still be deserialized. If a new error surfaces, fix it in a minimal follow-up edit. Do not submit until the notebook executes cleanly.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: checkpoint_ensembling_when_single_model_plateaus
rules.context: Multiple trained checkpoints (different epochs, architectures, or hyperparameters) are available, individual checkpoint scores are comparable with no single variant clearly dominating, and inference budget allows additional forward passes.
rules.action: Rather than selecting the single best checkpoint, average predictions from the top 2-3 diverse checkpoint variants and re-normalize. First test each individually; if neither clearly dominates, combine them. This typically yields a larger gain than further single-checkpoint search.
rules.exceptions: The ensembling benefit is inferred from trajectory in 52860091 rather than directly observed within that episode; rule assumes inference cost of extra forward passes is acceptable.

rules.name: lb_probing_when_cv_unreliable_for_selection
rules.context: You have a small number of model variants or checkpoints to choose from, and local CV scores are either unavailable or do not reliably predict leaderboard performance (e.g., CV-LB rank discordance observed, or no local metric available).
rules.action: Submit each variant individually to the leaderboard and record scores. Select the best performer based on LB rather than CV alone. After identifying the best single variant, consider ensembling the top LB performers. Expect small but meaningful score differences between variants.
rules.exceptions: When the number of variants is large, exhaustive LB probing may waste submissions. Also, if other pipeline variables are not controlled between submissions, single-checkpoint LB comparisons can be unreliable (as seen in 7606235 where the same fold yielded different scores across versions).

rules.name: tta_must_match_training_augmentation
rules.context: You have a trained model and want to apply test-time augmentation (TTA) using transformations (shifted crops, geometric augmentations) that the model may or may not have seen during training.
rules.action: Only apply TTA with transformations the model was trained on or that are deterministic/invertible (e.g., horizontal flip). If the model was trained with temporal crop augmentation, use multi-crop TTA (left/center/right) and average softmax outputs. If the model was trained only on center crops or without heavy geometric augmentation, avoid stochastic or out-of-distribution TTA (shifted windows, random rotations) as these likely add noise. Test TTA on one model group first; if score does not improve, revert rather than tuning TTA weights.
rules.exceptions: Earlier in 53424936 history, TTA helped even with models not explicitly trained on shifted crops, suggesting model architecture/capacity may sometimes compensate. The rule is model-dependent.

rules.name: swap_checkpoints_with_matched_config_and_verify
rules.context: You have multiple trained checkpoints (from different epochs, folds, or experiments) and want to select the best one(s) for inference without retraining.
rules.action: Swap in candidate checkpoints that show better validation metrics, but ensure inference-time architecture settings (e.g., dropout rate) match each checkpoint's training configuration. Verify each swap on the leaderboard before committing, as better validation metrics do not always transfer to better LB scores.
rules.exceptions: 49524919:e33#2 shows that checkpoints with better per-fold validation scores can yield worse LB (ConvNeXt at v150 scored 0.265), so always verify externally.

rules.name: probe_individual_models_to_improve_blend_checkpoints
rules.context: You have a multi-model ensemble/blend and want to both evaluate individual model contributions and improve the overall blend's checkpoint quality.
rules.action: When isolating each model group for standalone LB evaluation, simultaneously swap in updated checkpoint candidates for that group. After probing all groups, re-enable the full blend — it inherits any checkpoint improvements discovered during probing, potentially exceeding the pre-probe best score.
rules.exceptions: When multiple checkpoint changes are made simultaneously, it is unclear which contributed most to the improvement.

rules.name: repeated_submission_to_resolve_checkpoint_tie
rules.context: You have two top candidate checkpoints (or checkpoint sets) and leaderboard noise is high, making a single submission comparison unreliable.
rules.action: Submit each candidate multiple times and compare consistency across repeated submissions. Select the checkpoint that consistently scores better. Do not ensemble both if one is clearly weaker — a weaker model dilutes the stronger one.
rules.exceptions: none — only one kernel supports this; moving to singletons.

rules.name: swap_backbone_when_current_architecture_plateaus
rules.context: Performance has plateaued or regressed after tuning the current model's components (features, head architecture), and gains from incremental changes are diminishing or negative.
rules.action: Swap the model backbone (e.g., different boosting framework, different CNN/vision backbone) rather than continuing to tune the current one. Isolate the backbone change from other modifications, reduce iteration cost (e.g., fewer CV folds), and evaluate on CV before submitting. If a head simplification caused regression, try a stronger backbone with the simpler head before reverting.
rules.exceptions: In 55431616 the backbone swap was never submitted, so CV-competitiveness was not confirmed; the probe may have been abandoned, suggesting the swap does not always help.

rules.name: match_inference_resolution_to_model
rules.context: When running inference with a CNN (e.g., EfficientNet) and the test-time image resolution must be chosen, especially when switching between model checkpoints of different sizes.
rules.action: Derive the test-time image resolution from the model's expected input shape (e.g., canonical resolution for the variant, or programmatically from model.input.shape) rather than hardcoding an arbitrary value. Mismatched resolution can cause significant score drops (e.g., 0.957 → 0.945). When the model checkpoint changes, always update the resolution accordingly.
rules.exceptions: Auto-derived resolution may still produce poor scores if the model checkpoint itself failed to load correctly (13521245:e4#2).

rules.name: sweep_resolution_around_canonical_for_fine_detail_tasks
rules.context: When the task involves fine spatial detail (e.g., medical imaging with catheters/lines) and the model architecture accepts variable or multiple input resolutions, and you want to push accuracy beyond a working baseline.
rules.action: Start at the model's canonical or training resolution, then sweep in steps (one step above and below for EfficientNet variants, or ~100px steps for fully convolutional models). Submit each, pick the resolution that scores best. Two to three trials bracket the optimum. If a higher-resolution checkpoint exists, switch both weights and resolution simultaneously. Expect diminishing returns and possible degradation past a peak; stop when both neighbors of the current best are worse.
rules.exceptions: Changing both model architecture and resolution simultaneously confounds the signal (13577502:e3#1 v8). Single confirmation runs may not distinguish signal from noise when variance is ~0.002 (13702907:e8#1). The resolution effect may be small relative to model/training differences.
